42892356.label: Objective
42892356.text: Acute reactions to iodinated contrast material (ICM) and gadolinium-based contrast agents (GBCAs) are routinely encountered during CT and MR exams, but their associated direct medical costs and radiology practice workflow delays remain largely unknown. The purpose of this five-year, single-center retrospective study was to determine the costs and the Radiology departmental delays associated with acute ICM and GBCA reactions.

42892356.label: Methods
42892356.text: Contrast-enhanced CT and MR (CECT and CEMR) examinations performed from November 1, 2019, to October 31, 2024 at our institution were included. Acute reactions were identified as allergic-like or physiologic and categorized by severity using established ACR criteria. Drug, procedural, and hospitalization costs were estimated using 2025 CMS and US Department of Veterans Affairs databases. Delays were quantified by comparing time from exam start to departmental exit for exams with and without reactions.

42892356.label: Results
42892356.text: A total of 363,671 CECT exams and 253,860 CEMR exams were included, with 1099 acute ICM (789 allergic-like, 310 physiologic) and 521 acute GBCA reactions (321 allergic-like, 200 physiologic) identified. A minority of patients received billable medication or a procedure for their treatment (321 CECT, 29%; 107 CEMR, 21%). Median costs were modest ($15 for CECT; $1.66 for CEMR), but varied substantially by severity (severe reactions up to $238,029) and outcome (ED patient = $326, Admitted patient = $13,942). Acute ICM and GBCA reactions resulted in a median additional time of 25 minutes (IQR 11-43 min) and 27 minutes (IQR 8-59 min) in Radiology, respectively.

42892356.label: Conclusion
42892356.text: Acute ICM and GBCA reactions contribute to additional estimated direct medical costs and imaging delays that increase with reaction severity. Our findings help quantify how these adverse events increase direct and indirect estimated direct medical costs and negatively affect Radiology workflow; providing decision makers with important economic and operational context.

42975706.label: Objective
42975706.text: To develop and validate a noninvasive CT-based imaging score incorporating fractal analysis to predict high-risk pathological features in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and to assess its prognostic value for early recurrence.

42975706.label: Materials and methods
42975706.text: This retrospective bicenter study included 514 patients with pathologically confirmed PDAC who underwent curative resection, divided into training (n = 219), internal validation (n = 94), external validation (n = 100) and outcome datasets (n = 101). The fractal dimension (FD) and lacunarity were extracted from portal venous-phase CT images via box-counting algorithms. Imaging predictors of high-risk pathological features, including high tumor grade, lymphovascular invasion (LVI) and perineural invasion (PNI), were identified by logistic regression and integrated into a comprehensive weighted imaging score. Cox regression analyses were performed to assess its prognostic value for early recurrence.

42975706.label: Results
42975706.text: Patients with high-risk pathological features exhibited greater FD and lacunarity. The final score included six imaging features: necrosis, peripancreatic fat infiltration, venous involvement, regional lymphadenopathy, FD and lacunarity. For any high-risk pathology, the fractal-integrated score achieved AUC of 0.94, 0.88 and 0.84 in the training, internal validation and external validation datasets, respectively. For high pathological burden, the AUCs were 0.92, 0.80, and 0.77. In the outcome dataset, the score was an independent predictor of early recurrence (HR = 2.71; p = 0.004) and improved prognostic discrimination when combined with pathologic predictors.

42975706.label: Conclusion
42975706.text: This CT-based score, integrating fractal biomarkers, enables accurate, noninvasive preoperative prediction of aggressive pathological features in PDAC and provides incremental value for early recurrence risk stratification.

42975706.label: Key points
42975706.text: Question Can the fractal-based imaging features be used to predict high-risk pathological features and guide risk stratification for early recurrence in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)? Findings This CT-based score integrating fractal analysis predicted high-risk pathological features and was independent predictors of early recurrence and provided incremental prognostic value beyond pathologic factors. Clinical relevance This CT-based imaging score may help identify patients at high-risk of aggressive pathology before surgery and may further complement postoperative pathological risk stratification for early recurrence.

42993106.label: Background
42993106.text: Characteristics of future culprit lesions according to artificial intelligence-guided quantitative computed tomography (AI-QCT) are unknown.

42993106.label: Objectives
42993106.text: The authors aimed to characterize and derive thresholds to predict future culprit lesions from coronary computed tomography angiography using AI-QCT.

42993106.label: Methods
42993106.text: A total of 2,169 patients/13,772 lesions undergoing coronary computed tomography angiography at Turku University Hospital, Finland, (derivation) and 553 patients/3,948 lesions from Amsterdam University Medical Center, the Netherlands, (validation) were analyzed with AI-QCT. Lesions from vessels undergoing early revascularization were excluded. Lesion-level total plaque volume (TPV) and noncalcified plaque volume (NCPV) thresholds were derived and externally validated to predict lesion-level and patient-level acute coronary syndrome (ACS).

42993106.label: Results
42993106.text: Future culprit lesions from both cohorts (n = 69 validation; n = 15 derivation) had consistently higher median TPV (101 mm3 validation; 115 mm3 derivation; P = 0.811) and NCPV (65 mm3 validation; 74 mm3 derivation; P = 0.709) compared with control lesions (P < 0.001) and were nonobstructive in 69.6% (derivation) and 40.0% (validation). Thresholds of TPV ≥55 mm3 and NCPV ≥32 mm3 were derived and associated with significantly higher adjusted rates of lesion-level (TPV ≥55 mm3: adjusted HR: 12.09; 95% CI: 6.95-21.04; P < 0.001; NCPV ≥32 mm3: adjusted HR: 10.82; 95% CI: 6.22-18.80; P < 0.001) and patient-level ACS (TPV ≥55 mm3: adjusted HR: 2.92; 95% CI: 1.65-5.16; P < 0.001; NCPV ≥32 mm3: adjusted HR: 5.11; 95% CI: 2.49-10.46; P < 0.001) with consistent results in the validation cohort.

42993106.label: Conclusions
42993106.text: Future culprit lesions vs nonculprit lesions by AI-QCT demonstrated significantly higher plaque volumes and were nonobstructive in 40% to 70%. Thresholds of TPV ≥55 mm3 and NCPV ≥32 mm3 were derived to predict future culprit lesions and associated with increased rates of lesion-level and patient-level ACS in 2 independent cohorts.

43034256.label: Objectives
43034256.text: Infliximab (IFX) is a monoclonal antibody to treat Crohn's disease (CD), but loss of response is common. We aimed to develop an effective nomogram to predict long-term outcomes of IFX.

43034256.label: Materials and methods
43034256.text: A retrospective observational study was conducted on CD patients receiving regular IFX. The endpoint was defined as loss of response within 78 weeks, further classified as uncomplicated or complicated. Baseline characteristics, pre- and postinduction clinical indicators, and computed tomography enterography imaging features were collected. Candidate predictors were selected using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression and multivariable logistic regression to construct a clinical-radiological nomogram, validated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, decision curve analysis, and calibration plots. Kaplan-Meier analysis evaluated the clinical implications of predictor cut-off values.

43034256.label: Results
43034256.text: The study enrolled 165 patients, with 112 in the training cohort and 53 in the validation cohort. LASSO-logistic regression revealed erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) at week 14 and maximum small bowel wall thickness (SBWT-max) at baseline as independent predictors of long-term non-response. The nomogram achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.834 (training) and 0.913 (validation) for loss of response, and 0.746 and 0.876 for uncomplicated and complicated loss of response, respectively. Validation of the nomogram confirmed its discriminative, calibrating, and clinical utility. Additionally, ESR at week 14 > 10.5 mm/h or baseline SBWT-max > 7.5 mm showed reduced response duration.

43034256.label: Conclusions
43034256.text: The feasible nomogram combining ESR postinduction and SBWT-max at baseline effectively predicts long-term efficacy of IFX, which guides the therapy for CD patients.

43034256.label: Key points
43034256.text: QuestionLoss of response to infliximab is common in Crohn's disease, yet a reliable tool to predict long-term efficacy and guide timely therapeutic decisions remains rare. FindingsA nomogram based on LASSO-logistic regression integrating postinduction ESR and baseline maximum small bowel wall thickness accurately predicted long-term loss of response, including complicated failure. Clinical relevanceThis validated nomogram enables early, risk-stratified identification of patients likely to develop uncomplicated versus complicated loss of response, guiding proactive therapy switch and personalized management in Crohn's disease.

43058306.label: Background
43058306.text: Accurate interpretation of dopamine transporter (DAT)-SPECT depends on clinical context, including symptoms, medication, comorbidities, and structural imaging findings. In routine practice, however, this information is often documented as heterogeneous free text, which may hinder consistent consideration of clinically relevant parameters and limit guideline-compliant reporting. We therefore developed and evaluated a locally deployable small language model (SLM)-based pipeline to structure and standardize the clinical information section for DAT-SPECT reporting. Two retrospective datasets were used. The in-house dataset included clinical information sections from 2,990 DAT-SPECT examinations and was split into training (n = 2,700) and internal test data (n = 290). The external validation dataset comprised 595 clinical information sections from a second institution. A structured dictionary (466 entries across 12 categories) was created by two experienced DAT-SPECT readers and used to manually annotate the training and internal test samples. A Qwen3 1.7B model was fine-tuned by supervised learning to reproduce expert annotations. A rule-based postprocessing pipeline converted model outputs into report-ready structured text, including removal of redundant entries, automated suggestion of scan indication, consolidation of symptom lateralization and time course, reminders for missing guideline-relevant elements, and medication interaction checks. Internal test performance was assessed by expert comparison of SLM output with manual annotation. External performance was assessed by counting the manual corrections required in the postprocessed output under strict criteria.

43058306.label: Results
43058306.text: In the internal test dataset, the postprocessed SLM output provided the same information as the expert annotation in 196/290 cases (67.6%), including exact matches in 147/290 (50.7%). Interpretation differences due to free-text ambiguity occurred in 13/290 cases (4.5%), and SLM errors in 41/290 cases (14.1%). In 40/290 cases (13.8%), the SLM output was judged superior to the manual annotation. Among the error cases, 36/41 (87.8%) involved only a single erroneous or missing item. In the external dataset, 446/595 postprocessed outputs (75.0%) required no manual correction before inclusion in the report. Among the remaining 149/595 cases (25.0%), correction of only a single item was required in 111 cases (18.7% of all cases). The mean number of corrections was 0.34 items per case, corresponding to 6.0% of all structured items.

43058306.label: Conclusions
43058306.text: A locally deployable SLM combined with rule-based postprocessing can transform free-text clinical information for DAT-SPECT into standardized, report-ready documentation with good practical usability in an external dataset. End-to-end processing times of typically less than one second on the tested hardware support the feasibility of real-time local deployment. Prospective studies are required to determine its effects on clinical workflow and reporting quality.

43064856.label: Background
43064856.text: Photon-counting detector computed tomography (PCD-CT) enables native spectral imaging with the generation of virtual non-contrast (VNC) images from contrast-enhanced acquisitions. Two reconstruction algorithms are currently available, Virtual Unenhanced (VUE) and Liver Virtual Non-Contrast (LVNC), but their reliability compared with True Non-Contrast (TNC) imaging in abdominal applications remains incompletely established. This study evaluated the quantitative accuracy, image quality, and potential clinical impact of VNC reconstructions derived from PCD-CT.

43064856.label: Methods
43064856.text: In this retrospective single-center study, 150 patients, of whom 140 were included for the analyses, underwent multiphasic PCD-CT including TNC, arterial, and portal venous phases. VNC datasets were generated from arterial and venous acquisitions using the VUE and LVNC algorithms. Tissue attenuation, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) were compared with TNC images. The agreement of VNC reconstructions with TNC-based classification criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis, and osteoporosis was also evaluated.

43064856.label: Results
43064856.text: Significant attenuation differences were observed between TNC and VNC reconstructions across most tissues. The smallest errors were found in soft tissues, particularly the liver and spleen, whereas the largest discrepancies occurred in vascular and osseous structures. SNR was higher on VNC than on TNC images in the liver, spleen and paravertebral muscle but lower in several other tissues, whereas CNR was higher with LVNCa and lower with VUEv than with TNC. VUE most closely reproduced TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs. Agreement with TNC-based criteria for hepatic steatosis, myosteatosis and osteoporosis required reconstruction-specific cut-offs, which should be considered exploratory. Omitting TNC could potentially reduce radiation exposure by 16.5% for upper abdomen and 21.2% for total abdominal examinations.

43064856.label: Conclusions
43064856.text: VUE reconstructions showed good agreement with TNC attenuation in the liver and spleen in both contrast phases, whereas LVNC systematically underestimated attenuation in iodine-enhancing organs and was closer to TNC than VUE only in subcutaneous fat and venous-phase muscle. Substantial bias in vascular and bone structures limits the interchangeability of both algorithms with TNC imaging. VNC may support a potential reduction in radiation dose when replacing a planned TNC acquisition; since lesion detection and characterization were not evaluated, the safe omission of TNC was not demonstrated.
